name: Sara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead crew for the electricity company out on the peninsula, which is basically forty miles of lines along the coast that the salt and wind try to eat. Normal day is replacing corroded insulators, fixing a line a gull or a gale has brought down, re-tensioning spans. For the last year I've also been one of the two drone pilots for our depot, flying the lines to spot damage before we climb.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up flying the drone?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put my hand up when nobody else would. I'd been using AI on my phone every day anyway, to plan jobs, check manuals, even to help Finn with his reading because he's dyslexic, so a drone felt like the next toy. Pay didn't change, mind you, which still annoys me, because Owen's library hours got cut and we're scraping by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that it's still useful, because the drone saves us climbing to check things that turn out fine. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype was mostly the big tech companies selling shares. I'd still be the one telling the lads to try the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine, but I'd be a bit let down. I liked the idea that the boring, dangerous bits get handed off. If nothing changes, I'm still a lower-paid lineworker on a windy coast with a mortgage we can barely cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep using the tools I use now. I'd push the union to get drone pilots recognised as a proper grade with an allowance, because right now I do two jobs for one wage. And I'd keep teaching the newer lads how to read the drone images.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little sigh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the allowance worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we got the same as the inspectors in the city, it'd be about a hundred and fifty a month. That's the difference between topping up the car and not. I've already asked twice and been told "after the review".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Finn and Hattie about AI in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's a good tool, like a good drill, and it's not magic. Finn uses it to read his history books aloud and that's made a huge difference to his marks. I'd want them to keep using it like that.

S0.say: She'd say the tools are still useful because the drone saves pointless climbs. Online she'd post that the hype was mostly big tech companies selling shares.
S0.think: She'd be a little let down, because she liked the idea of handing off the boring and dangerous bits. She'd still be a lower-paid lineworker on a windy coast with a mortgage they can barely cover.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI tools and drone she already uses and pushes the union for a drone pilot allowance worth about a hundred and fifty a month. Keeps training newer crew to read drone images.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm still a lower-paid lineworker on a windy coast with a mortgage we can barely cover.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is the rare worker who would be disappointed by a plateau. Her frustration is about pay for the extra skill she's already taken on. Her son's dyslexia gives her a very personal reason to value AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that sounds like where we're headed anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is coming and we should shape it, not just complain about it. At the union meeting I'd say get in early and write the rules, or the company writes them for us. Online I'd share stuff about workers being trained for the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I already fly the drone and use the software, so I'm the one they'll need when inspections go mostly automatic. The worry is whether the company pays for that skill or just expects it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my advanced drone licence in the first six months, the one for flying beyond sight along the coast. I'd learn the fault-prediction software the minute they bring it in. And I'd push hard for the union to set the pay for these roles before management does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. The money worry sits in the background, it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's good for you. Who on the crew is it bad for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Dave, who's done twenty-five years and won't touch a tablet. He knows those coast lines better than any drone ever will, but nobody's going to pay him for that. I'd want the union to find a role for people like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The advanced licence costs money. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six hundred. I'd ask the company first, and if they say no, I'd pay for it in two goes and skip our week away in August. Owen would grumble but he'd understand.

S1.say: She'd say the change is coming and workers should shape it instead of just complaining. She'd urge the union to get in early and write the rules before the company does.
S1.think: She thinks it's good for her because she already flies the drone and uses the software. Her worry is whether the company will pay for that skill or just expect it.
S1.do: Gets an advanced beyond-sight drone licence within six months, paying the six hundred herself if needed and skipping the August holiday. Learns fault-prediction software as soon as it arrives and presses the union to set pay for the new roles.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit excited, with the money worry sitting in the background.
S1.quote: At the union meeting I'd say get in early and write the rules, or the company writes them for us.
S1.fieldNote: She combines enthusiasm for the technology with a firm belief in union bargaining. Her concern for an older colleague shows she sees who loses out. She'd pay for her own training even with almost no savings, which says a lot about her appetite for risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs a huge public response, like a war-time effort, with the gains shared out instead of going to a few companies. At work I'd tell people we need to be in the room when the robots arrive. Online I'd be posting about it all the time, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being quick with the tools only buys me a little time. For a year or two they'd need people like me to set up the robots and check what the drones see. After that, if the AI is better and cheaper at everything, my being keen doesn't save the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to whatever team rolls out the robots on our network, because that's where the last human jobs would be for a while. I'd cut back hard at home, no holiday, cheaper phone plans, so we had a few weeks in the bank. And I'd be at the union every week pushing for a deal that shares the savings with the workers they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and scared at the same time, which is a strange mix to sleep on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being keen doesn't save the mortgage. So what would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some kind of public income, honestly, paid for by taxing the companies that own the robots. If the machines are doing all the work, the money has to come back somehow. Otherwise it's just the same few people getting richer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hattie, who's eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her Mum's helping the robots learn our lines, which is true for a while. I wouldn't want her worried. She'd probably ask if the robot can fix her bike.

S2.say: She'd call for a war-time-scale public response with the gains shared instead of going to a few companies. At work she'd say lineworkers need to be in the room when robots arrive.
S2.think: Privately she knows being quick with tools buys only a year or two setting up robots. After that, if AI is better and cheaper at everything, being keen doesn't save the mortgage.
S2.do: Applies at once to the team rolling out robots on her network and cuts the holiday and phone plans to build a few weeks of savings. Pushes the union weekly for a deal sharing the savings with laid-off workers.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited and scared at the same time.
S2.quote: After that, if the AI is better and cheaper at everything, my being keen doesn't save the mortgage.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability gives her a short head start, and she's honest that it's only that. She feels some control because she knows exactly where she'd apply. Her answer for the long term is political, a public income funded by robot owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about sharing the gains, but with more hope in it. Five years is a full election cycle, so I'd tell people to vote for whoever has a plan for workers. At the depot I'd say let's get the training sorted now, while the company still needs us and we've got some bargaining power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to get a proper qualification. I'd be one of the first ones the company calls when they test robots on live lines. That's a few good years of work, and maybe a role running a robot crew for longer than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the two-year online diploma in grid automation the first month, evenings and Sundays. I'd start putting fifty a week aside. And I'd volunteer for every robot trial the company runs, even the ugly early ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like the night before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said keen doesn't save the mortgage. Does five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In five years I can pay a chunk off and be properly qualified before the end comes. It doesn't change where it ends, but it changes whether I'm standing or flat on my back when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Evenings and Sundays on top of call-outs. What does Owen say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm mad, and then he'd do the Sunday dinners. He did it when I did my apprenticeship exams. We're a good team when we've got a plan.

S3.say: She'd say the gains must be shared but with more hope, urging people to vote for whoever has a plan for workers. At the depot she'd push to sort training while workers still have bargaining power.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough for a proper qualification and to be first called for live-line robot trials. That could mean a few good years and maybe a role running a robot crew.
S3.do: Enrols in a two-year online grid automation diploma in the first month, studying evenings and Sundays. Saves fifty a week and volunteers for every robot trial the company runs.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like the night before a new job.
S3.quote: It doesn't change where it ends, but it changes whether I'm standing or flat on my back when it does.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her into a planner with a clear qualification in mind. She's alert to timing, seeing that bargaining power lasts only while the company still needs crews. She relies on her partner's support to make the plan work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Finn would be twenty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. I'd say it at the union, at the school, wherever. I'd want public training funds open to everyone, not just the people with time and money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels mostly fine for me personally. I'd have time to retrain, get the kids through school and maybe pay a real chunk off the mortgage. What bothers me is what happens to the Big Daves, and whether there's anything left for Finn and Hattie to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the grid automation diploma slowly, over three years. I'd talk to Finn about what to study, maybe something where he's working with people, or robotics if he likes it. I'd keep saving and keep pushing the union and politicians for a fund that pays everyone's retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, mostly for other people. For me it's more curiosity than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been hopeful through all of these. Is there a version of this decade that scares you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the one where the companies take ten years of warning and do nothing but buy up robots and lobby. Then it's the two-year picture, just in slow motion. That would make me furious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Finn to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever he loves, honestly. If AI can do almost anything, then the thing that matters is whether he's happy and decent. That sounds soft for a lineworker, I know.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is plenty of time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. She'd want public training funds open to everyone, not just people with time and money.
S4.think: Personally ten years feels mostly fine: time to retrain, get the kids through school and pay down the mortgage. What bothers her is older colleagues and what's left for her children to do.
S4.do: Takes the grid automation diploma slowly over three years and talks with her son about studying people work or robotics. Keeps saving and lobbies the union and politicians for a fund that pays for everyone's retraining.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly on behalf of others, with more curiosity than fear.
S4.quote: Then it's the two-year picture, just in slow motion.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her worry shifts almost entirely to other people. Her biggest fear is that companies waste the warning time. Her advice to her son, to follow what he loves, surprised her as much as me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to turn being keen into anything solid. What would help is paid training that starts now, a proper allowance for the skills people are already learning, and some kind of public income so the robots' earnings come back to the people they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the drone has taught me. The lines look completely different from above. You see where the salt's eating everything. I'd like people to remember that somebody has to know what they're looking at.

headlineQuote: I'd tell her Mum's helping the robots learn our lines, which is true for a while.
portrait: Sara Evans is a 43-year-old overhead lineworker on a salt-eaten coastal peninsula who volunteered to be her depot's drone pilot and uses AI every day, including to help her dyslexic son read. Money is tight since her partner's library hours were cut, and she resents doing two jobs for one wage. She'd be disappointed by a plateau and is mostly excited by steady change. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because her head start only buys a year or two, while five and ten years let her plan a grid automation diploma. Her answer for the end point is political: share the robots' earnings with the people they replace.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to turn her early skills into anything solid before the mortgage is at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training that starts now, a proper allowance for skills people are already learning, and a public income funded by the robots' earnings.
